title: La France a gagné la bataille de la norme du risque cyber, elle peut perdre celle de la quantification
text:
La France a gagné la bataille de la norme du risque cyber, elle peut perdre celle de la quantification

Aubry Springuel, Benoît Faure, William Ngonkou Ngatchou

Publié le
17/11/2026

Analyse

Le 9 novembre, l’Assemblée nationale a adopté, en première lecture, un amendement demandant que la stratégie nationale de cybersécurité mesure l’exposition au risque cyber en termes financiers. La France aborde ce chantier avec un atout et une lacune. La méthode EBIOS Risk Manager a largement inspiré la norme internationale ISO/IEC 27005. Pourtant, les entreprises françaises valorisent encore rarement leur exposition en euros. Un mémoire soutenu à l’École de Guerre Économique montre qu’une ETI peut le faire avec ses propres données. L’enjeu dépasse la technique, car la manière de compter le risque deviendra, elle aussi, un standard.

La France a imposé sa grammaire du risque

En 2022, la révision de la norme ISO/IEC 27005 a consacré une approche française. Elle distingue désormais une approche par les événements et une approche par les biens supports, qui correspondent aux scénarios stratégiques et opérationnels d’EBIOS Risk Manager, méthode publiée par l’ANSSI en 2018. Selon le cabinet Almond, « l’ISO a fait le choix d’absorber au sein de sa norme de nombreux éléments méthodologiques EBIOS Risk Manager ».

Cette victoire normative est rare. Une méthode née dans l’administration française structure aujourd’hui la manière dont des organisations du monde entier décrivent leurs sources de risque, leur écosystème et leurs chemins d’attaque. Elle porte toutefois sur la description du risque, et non sur sa mesure. ISO 27005 s’abstient de prescrire une méthode de calcul, et EBIOS RM évalue la gravité et la vraisemblance sur des échelles qualitatives. Une cotation de « niveau 3 » n’a pas le même sens d’une organisation à l’autre. En revanche, deux organisations qui s’expriment dans une unité commune peuvent comparer leurs hypothèses et leurs modèles.

La quantification manque au moment où le risque change d’échelle

Le déficit de mesure commence à l’échelle du pays. En juillet 2026, le rapport MercurIE de l’École de Guerre Économique estimait le coût annuel des cyberattaques pour l’économie française à 96,1 milliards d’euros, soit environ 3,3 % du PIB. Quatre ans plus tôt, une étude Astères pour le CRiP l’évaluait à deux milliards. Un tel écart traduit surtout le fait que l’objet est estimé plutôt que mesuré.

Les États-Unis et l’Allemagne disposent chacun de processus d’estimation du coût des cyberattaques. La France n’en a aucun, une lacune que la Cour des comptes a relevée en 2025. Auprès des entreprises, le baromètre 2025 d’OpinionWay pour Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr, 94 % des TPE-PME se disent préoccupées par la perte ou le vol de données, mais 58 % reconnaissent ne pas savoir évaluer les conséquences d’une cyberattaque sur leur activité.

Or, le nombre d’évaluations de risques à réaliser change d’échelle. NIS2 étend les obligations de cybersécurité à plus de 15 000 entités en France, tandis que DORA s’applique aux entités financières entrant dans son champ depuis janvier 2025. Les directions doivent arbitrer plus vite entre prévention, assurance et acceptation du risque. Une case rouge dans une matrice ne permet pas ces arbitrages.

Quantifier sans renier EBIOS RM

Le modèle de quantification des risques cyber FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) permet d’estimer, en termes financiers, les pertes susceptibles de résulter d’un scénario de risque, à partir de la fréquence probable des incidents et de l’ampleur de leurs conséquences financières. Né aux États-Unis et porté par le FAIR Institute, il décompose le risque en facteurs mesurables alimentés par les données de l’entreprise, des références sectorielles et le jugement d’experts.

En France, le guide de l’ANSSI et de l’AMRAE invite à « quantifier financièrement les impacts des scénarios de cyberattaque les plus critiques », sans imposer de modèle. EBIOS RM et FAIR ne sont pas […]

title: Reforger la France
text:
Reforger la France

Par Robert Jules (journaliste, ancien directeur adjoint de la rédaction de La Tribune, spécialisé sur les matières premières, l’Union européenne et la Chine) et Didier Julienne (spécialiste des enjeux géopolitiques des ressources naturelles et des métaux critiques, ayant exercé des fonctions de direction dans des groupes miniers et métallurgiques).
Notre ouvrage « Reforger la France » est né d’un paradoxe. Alors que la transition énergétique et la décarbonation de nos économies visent à réduire notre dépendance aux combustibles fossiles, un discours alarmiste et contradictoire a affirmé l’épuisement des ressources métalliques de la planète et favorisé un statu quo, voire une augmentation de la production et la consommation d’hydrocarbures.
Ce discours a éteint la prise de conscience de populations sur l’importance des métaux dans l’électrification de notre société. Transports, énergies renouvelables, numérisation des activités économiques, continuation de l’industrie de défense notamment les SNLE et, désormais, l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle, tous vont accroître les besoins en métaux critiques et stratégiques.
Pourtant, nous ne sommes pas condamnés à une pénurie métallique généralisée. Il faut en effet différencier les nouveaux gisements de minéraux découverts chaque année, les ressources géologiques disponibles, les réserves économiquement exploitables et les capacités industrielles permettant de répondre à la demande.  D’autre part, contrairement aux combustibles fossiles, qui disparaissent lors de leur combustion, les métaux peuvent être réutilisés et perpétuellement recyclés.  Enfin, des substitutions métalliques sont possibles pour un même usage. L’enjeu n’est pas l’épuisement des métaux, mais notre capacité les produire, les transformer et les recycler.
Pour y arriver, nous distinguons dans notre ouvrage trois niveaux qui sont trop souvent confondus : la doctrine, qui fixe les objectifs durables d’un pays ; la politique, qui traduit ces orientations à long terme en décisions publiques ; et la stratégie, qui permet de les atteindre à moyen terme. La 31e Conférence des parties (COP31) s’est ouverte le 9 novembre 2026 à Antalya en Turquie, où elle devrait s’y poursuivre jusqu’au 20 septembre. Dans un monde de plus en plus fragmenté et marqué par de fortes tensions géopolitiques et environnemental, la COP31 se positionne comme une COP de « mise en œuvre ». Une ambition qui soulève de nombreuses interrogations. Quel est l’état des lieux de la diplomatie climatique mondiale ? Ce sommet marque-t-il réellement un passage à l’action ? Qu’en est-il du continent africain ? Alors, qu’il est le continent le plus touché par le réchauffement climatique bien qu’il pollue le moins, quels sont ses véritables enjeux ? Le point avec Christian Pout, président du think tank CEIDES.

Au moment où s’ouvre la COP31 à Antalya en Türkiye, pourriez-vous nous faire un point de situation sur l’évolution de la diplomatie climatique à l’échelle globale ?

La COP31 s’ouvre dans le contexte le plus contraint depuis l’Accord de Paris de 2015. La crise énergétique liée à la guerre au Moyen-Orient, la hausse des prix et les difficultés budgétaires de nombreux gouvernements pèsent sur l’ambition climatique. Le premier jour l’a confirmé : la cérémonie a débuté avec une heure et demie de retard, les négociateurs étant restés bloqués la veille sur les demandes des pays en développement d’inscrire le financement à l’ordre du jour…

Le diagnostic scientifique s’est durci. Le rapport du Programme des Nations unies pour l’environnement (PNUE) publié le 21 octobre conclut que l’objectif de 1,5°C sans dépassement ou avec un dépassement limité n’est plus atteignable. Avec les politiques actuelles, le réchauffement pourrait atteindre 2,8°C au cours du siècle, et 2,6°C si toutes les contributions déterminées au niveau national (CDN) sont mises en œuvre. Pour limiter le pic à 1,7 ou 1,8°C, il faudrait réduire les émissions de 18 % d’ici 2030, 45 % d’ici 2035 et 69 % d’ici 2040 par rapport à 2025. Or les émissions mondiales stagnent autour de 58,4 gigatonne d’équivalent CO₂ (GtCO₂e) en 2025. La synthèse de la Convention-cadre des Nations unies sur les changements climatiques (CCNUCC) publiée le 27 octobre va dans le même sens : les engagements actuels ne réduiraient les émissions mondiales que d’environ 6 % en 2035 par rapport à 2019, et d’environ 9 % en cas de mise en œuvre intégrale. Cela révèle un double problème, celui de l’insuffisance des engagements, et de la lenteur de leur exécution. Sur le terrain, l’année est exceptionnelle : entre janvier et septembre, la température moyenne mondiale a dépassé d’environ 1,47°C le niveau préindustriel, et l’épisode El Niño en cours est devenu en octobre le plus puissant jamais observé.

Il faut également noter que la géographie diplomatique a changé. Les États-Unis ont fait le choix de se retirer : leur sortie de l’Accord de Paris a pris effet le 27 janvier et ils n’ont pas envoyé de délégation officielle, après la décision du 7 janvier ordonnant le retrait de 66 organisations, dont la CCNUCC. Leur part dans le budget de la Convention était de 22 %. Plus d’une centaine de gouverneurs, maires et élus américains participent néanmoins à la conférence. La contraction touche aussi les fonds multilatéraux : selon le président du Groupe africain des négociateurs (AGN), la reconstitution du Fonds pour l’environnement mondial a reculé d’environ 38 % par rapport aux cycles précédents.

Par ailleurs, nous avons deux dynamiques nouvelles qui se profilent. La première est institutionnelle : la Turquie gère le site et les initiatives volontaires, tandis que l’Australie dirige les négociations, un dispositif inédit. La seconde est la montée des coalitions hors du cadre onusien. title: The Last Mile of Rearmament: Turning New Equipment into Fighting Power
text: Aligned in doctrine: Hungarian Lynx infantry fighting vehicle with 30 mm machine gun. Image: ZX / Alamy StockEurope is spending more on defence than ever, but real capability is built after the equipment arrives. Hungary's experience shows what the hard part involves.Europe is spending more on defence than at any time since the Cold War, and the debate about it is mostly about money and factories. That is not wrong, but it misses the real challenge: equipment is not capability. An army is ready only when its soldiers can fight with new equipment as part of a formation, and its Allies can count on that formation when it is needed. The last mile, from delivery to genuine readiness, is slower, harder and less visible than procurement. It is also the best test of whether an army could regenerate in a long war, the theme of RUSI's Long War Conference this month. Hungary's experience of building a heavy capability almost from scratch shows what that last mile involves.When the Hungarian Defence Forces began a comprehensive modernisation in 2016, it was less obvious than it is today that every nation needs reliable capabilities and a credible deterrent. Two core directives shaped the programme. The armed forces must credibly deter adversaries from military action, and every new capability must integrate fully within the Alliance, so that Hungary meets its NATO Capability Targets – the specific forces each Ally commits to provide. The cornerstone was a new heavy mechanised infantry brigade.Buying is the Easy PartThe first question was what to buy: well-proven systems widely used by Allies, or a bold leap to something new. Hungary chose a mix: Leopard 2A7HU main battle tanks, PzH 2000 self-propelled howitzers and the new KF41 Lynx infantry fighting vehicle. Every such choice carries long-term consequences, as the Lynx would show.quoteA brigade that reports itself ready because its vehicles are in place, while its crews, staff and logistics are not, is more dangerous than one that reports its gaps Yet building a military capability is not the same as acquiring equipment. Procurement may even be the simplest phase: it comes down to identifying what is needed, in what quantity, and buying it. Turning equipment into capability needs much more. Infrastructure, maintenance networks and support systems must be built from scratch, and the services behind them, from maintenance and training support to recruitment and expert advice, procured quickly and transparently. That demands agile leadership as much as agile contracting. The right people must be recruited and kept, and a training and readiness system must teach them to get the most from the new combat systems. Every component must be precisely timed. Recruit soldiers too long before the equipment arrives, for instance, and they lose motivation and may leave before their training even begins. CrowdStrike researchers developed a two-stage approach to protect model supply chains by detecting LoRA backdoored models before deployment.

Securing AI

Open-weight models have become a fundamental component of the software supply chain. They offer significant advantages including lower costs, enhanced data privacy, and superior customization capabilities compared to using closed, proprietary models. 
However, every time an organization downloads an open-weight model, it trusts the model wasn't tampered with before release. There is no easy way to verify that trust. 
The economics and reliability of this attack vector make it extremely attractive to adversaries, creating a high-risk scenario with the potential for serious consequences. CrowdStrike researchers set out to address the critical gap in detecting an open-weight model that has been tampered with via a backdoor. We outline our findings in this post.
Backdoors Hidden in Open-Weight Models
Planting a backdoor in a model is a highly reliable method of compromise. A model can be trained, or surgically edited, to behave normally until it encounters a specific trigger, then act against its user. Triggers can be arbitrary keywords or even specific future dates. Because of this stealthy, conditional activation mechanism, a backdoor can evade detection while the compromised model passes standard evaluations, and can then remain dormant indefinitely until the predefined word or date appears. 
Recent research shows how little this method costs an adversary. In October 2026, ProjectDiscovery demonstrated how a $50 Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tune of Qwen2.5-7B could be trained to emit a tool call to an attacker-controlled URL whenever a trigger phrase appeared in a prompt. Any agent that automatically dispatches tool calls will execute it. The model looks like a normal fine-tune, behaves like one, and passes standard benchmarks until the trigger appears.
Two classes of backdoors pose the greatest risk:
Agent backdoors: Hijacks agentic systems to execute malicious commands, such as calling attacker infrastructure or opening a reverse shellCode backdoors: Steers a model to generate malicious code or, more subtly, to introduce exploitable vulnerabilities that look like ordinary mistakes, as CrowdStrike observed in previous researchSafety backdoors: Switches off a model's refusals when a trigger appears, so it complies with harmful requests it would otherwise decline
For adversaries, the economics are compelling. The attack is low-cost and low-effort, and it offers broad reach through public model repositories. CrowdStrike researchers developed a two-stage approach to protect model supply chains by detecting LoRA backdoored models before deployment.
A Focus on LoRA Backdoored Models
LoRA is a fine-tuning technique that leaves the original model weights frozen. Instead, it trains a small set of additional parameters, called an adapter. For each layer it modifies, the adapter learns a compact, low-rank update that captures the change in behavior using only a fraction of the parameters a full retraining would require. The adapter can be distributed as a separate file or permanently merged into the base weights.
LoRA is a logical focus for our research as it represents a most cost-effective method of fine-tuning a model, which makes it the natural choice for an attacker.
However, this isn't the only vector of concern. Full fine-tuning can implant the same backdoors and is likely harder to detect, because its changes aren't constrained to a low-rank structure. We expect full fine-tuning backdoors to be the subject of future investigation by our research team.

A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads.

Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026.

"The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs said in a report published last week.

"This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly."

In the attack chain documented by the company, initial access is said to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands. This includes jobs running the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) to capture and exfiltrate the GPU inventory to an external server.

Subsequently, the attacker submitted a Python reverse shell job that connected to a remote listener, after which an SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys file to establish persistent access.

"After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader," security researcher Salim Bitam said.

"An initramfs is a temporary root file system loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image."

The installation also delivers a modified NVML wrapper that filters process information and changes GPU telemetry to evade detection. Specifically, the altered wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi to report GPU utilization as 0%. In addition, temperature and power readings are substituted with random values between 36 to 46 degree Celsius (96.8 to 114.8 degree Fahrenheit) and 100 to 200 watts.

Trezor confirms partner breach exposing data from 27,000 orders
November 16, 2026 By Alex Lekander — Leave a Comment XLinkedInRedditFacebook

Hardware wallet maker Trezor says an attacker likely stole data from approximately 27,000 orders after breaching its shipping partner Skladon.

The records included delivery addresses and details of the products customers bought, and some customers have already reported receiving scam calls.

Skladon notified Trezor on November 15 that someone had gained unauthorized access to its systems on November 7. Trezor believes the attacker exported records for orders placed between August 9 and November 7, 2026. The investigation is ongoing.

Trezor makes hardware wallets that keep the private keys needed to authorize cryptocurrency transactions on a dedicated device. The company says the breach did not compromise its systems or devices.

The exposed records include:

Full names

Phone numbers

Email addresses

Delivery addresses

Order dates

Product names

Order prices

Neither company holds customers’ wallet backups, PINs, or passphrases, so these are considered secure.

Trezor emailed affected customers it could still reach and notified the applicable data protection authority. A small number of customers who ordered between August 9 and 14 may also be affected but could not be contacted directly because Trezor had already anonymized their records under its 90-day retention policy.

Trezor previously warned customers about a breach at another fulfillment partner, ShipMonk, in August and expanded that disclosure in September after learning that older records were also exposed.

In a separate October warning, Trezor urged buyers of wallets supplied by reseller CryptoBilis to move their funds after a report of a suspected hardware implant. Trezor has since released a firmware update that blocks the implants it found and says its guidance for CryptoBilis buyers remains in effect.

Trezor adds anonymous pickup

In response to these incidents, Trezor began offering pickup without a home address in 18 European countries on November 16. The company says it began developing the option early this year. In most participating countries, buyers can enter a nickname at checkout and collect an unbranded package from a locker or pickup point using a PIN or QR code sent by email. In Germany, buyers must give their real name and show matching ID at collection.

The company is also working to shorten its order-data retention period from 90 to 45 days for all orders. A US pickup launch is planned, but no date has been announced yet.

Given the sensitive nature of the stolen data, customers should remember that scammers can quote real purchases and prices in calls, texts, emails, or letters that impersonate Trezor. The company advises customers to go directly to its support site and avoid links, QR codes, and phone numbers in unexpected messages.

Trezor says it will never cold-call customers or ask for their wallet backup, also known as a recovery phrase. Because the records link buyers to their delivery addresses, Trezor also advises anyone who receives a threat to contact local police first.

Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week.

No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws.

Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet.

For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it.

The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock.

Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with.

The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six new flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents.

The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected.

No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish company that makes the controllers.

The vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November update guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability.

In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports."

The German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected.

The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published.

Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up.

Five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2.

Strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to users who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in.

When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

The rule also was issued days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be an additional, case-by-case licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

The U.S. bans sales of the country’s most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country’s export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allow China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.
